extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Tatler / coffee-house literati; actors and playgoers; letter-writers and social observers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria (drawn from Hamlet's advice and Tatler essays) for actors' delivery and forstanders' conversational/letter-writing decorum; aimed at helping theatre audiences and social readers judge performance, speech, and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of action for actors (Hamlet's directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak the speech as I pronounce it to you, trippingly on the tongue; but if you mouth it, as many of our players do, I had as lieve the town-crier had spoke my lines: nor do not saw the air too much with your hand thus; but use all gently: for in the very torrent, tempest, and...whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that may give it smoothness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full set of practical rules for acting taken from Hamlet and applied as a judgement framework: (a) speak the lines naturally and 'trippingly', not by mouthing or over-enunciating; (b) avoid excessive gesticulation ('saw the air') — use gestures gently; (c) even in violent passions preserve temperance to give smoothness; (d) avoid tearing a passion 'to tatters' or overdoing to the point of grotesque display; (e) do not be too tame either — use discretion and balance; (f) 'suit the action to the word, the word to the action' and avoid overstepping 'the modesty of nature'; (g) reform strutting, bellowing, and unnatural accents which imitate humanity abominably; (h) players portraying clowns should not ad-lib or speak more than is set down for them to manufacture cheap laughter. Examples/anti-patterns: actors who 'mouth' lines, 'tear a passion to tatters', strut and bellow, or induce inappropriate laughter from 'groundlings' are singled out as failures. Use these points to judge an actor's fidelity to naturalness, verbal-gesture coordination, and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overacting / over-emoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything so overdone, is from the purpose of playing, whose end...was, and is, to hold as it were the mirror up to Nature;...This overdone, or come tardy off, though it make the unskilful laugh, cannot but make the judicious grieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting should mirror Nature; over-exaggeration (overdoing, 'out-Herods Herod') is an anti-pattern that pleases the unskilful but grieves the judicious. Evaluate performances for proportion: intensity should be appropriate to text and character, not mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit action to the word; word to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Suit the action to the word, the word to the action; with this special observance, that you overstep not the modesty of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key evaluative principle: gesture and movement must match the verbal content and emotional truth of the line; mechanical or mismatched action (gestures that do not arise from the text) is a fault. Also ensure natural modesty — avoid excesses that break verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clown/Comic restraint — no self-aggrandising improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Let those that play your clowns, speak no more than is set down for them: for there be of them that will of themselves laugh, to set on some quantity of barren spectators to laugh too; though in the meantime, some necessary question of the play be then to be considered; that is villanous, and shows a most pitiful ambition in the fool that uses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic performers should not improvise or insert antics that derail plot or timing merely to elicit cheap laughs. Evaluate comic actors on their service to the play and the audience's understanding rather than on isolated guffaws they provoke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and sincerity in lover's letters
rubrics_metrics.description: As I know no reason why difference of sex should make our language to each other differ from the ordinary rules of right reason, I shall affect plainness and sincerity in my discourse to you, as much as other lovers do perplexity and rapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model for composing courtship correspondence: favour straightforward, sincere expression over rhetorical excesses and inflated hyperbole (e.g., avoid 'I shall die for you'); wait to declare deep sentiments until you know how they will be received; promise realistic commitments ('I should be glad to lead my life with you') rather than melodramatic vows. Use tone of deference and measured familiarity appropriate to the social situation (example letter provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's historical/occasional writing: truth and simplicity over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: History therefore written by a woman...it will not...be demanded, that style and ornament shall be so much consulted, as truth and simplicity; which latter qualities we may more justly pretend to beyond the other sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing accounts (here: 'history written by a woman'), prioritize faithful, simple narration of facts and motives (especially about love and social relations) rather than ornate style. The piece's purpose is clarity of social truth rather than rhetorical flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation/speech etiquette — avoid superfluous discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: I have...been led into the consideration of the use of speech...to know to which I may more justly impute the sin of superfluous discourse...Expect therefore to hear of the whisperer without business, the laugher without wit, the complainer without receiving injuries, and a very large crowd...whose tongues are too voluble for their brains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative yardstick for social conversation: judge speakers by relevance, restraint, and wit. Anti-patterns include voluble talkers who speak without cause, laughers without wit, complainers who have no injury, and loud boors who disturb assemblies. Balance, appropriateness to occasion, and mental substance are virtues; excessive fluency without thought is censured. Examples: country squires who 'roar' instead of speak (Tom Bellfrey) are mocked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social signifiers: taking snuff as indicator of vacuity
rubrics_metrics.description: My method...I sat by an eminent story-teller and politician who takes half an ounce in five seconds...I took his box to see how long you could live without it...I observed that his dulness was much more regular and fluent than before. A pinch supplied the place of, 'As I was saying,' 'And so, sir'...taking snuff is done only to supply with sensations the want of reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social habit critique: taking snuff (especially borrowing snuff) is portrayed as a gesture that masks lack of thought and supplies sensations to cover emptiness. Use this as a sociable evaluative cue: habitual snuff-taking signals frivolity or paucity of reflection; borrowers of snuff are viewed as particularly pitiable. This is normative social commentary for judging interlocutors' intellectual presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiring a gentlewoman's maid: whispering, lisp, and soft tread
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentlewoman who has a very delicate ear, wants a maid who can whisper, and help her in the government of her family. If the said servant can clear-starch, lisp, and tread softly, she shall have suitable encouragement in her wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small prescriptive rubric (comic and practical): for certain genteel households, desirable servant skills include whispering ability, skill in starching linen, a lisp (to deliver controlled whispers), and soft tread. These are practical selection criteria for domestic hiring in the social milieu described.
